name: Oscillations: mean position, displacement and amplitude
subtopic: Oscillations: mean position, displacement and amplitude
summary: In an oscillation, displacement is measured from the mean (equilibrium) position, and the amplitude is the maximum displacement: the distance from the mean position to either extreme, which is half the extreme-to-extreme distance.
learning_objective: Students will be able to locate the mean position of an oscillating body, measure displacement from it, find the amplitude as half the distance between the extreme positions, and tell periodic, oscillatory and simple harmonic motion apart.

contrast_probes.probe: What would you need to check before saying a repeating motion is 'SHM with an amplitude of 5 cm'?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: That it is SHM, and that its two ends are 5 cm apart.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Only that it repeats at equal intervals, and that it goes 5 cm out from the middle.

contrast_probes.probe: A pendulum released from one extreme swings between extremes 8 cm apart; what is its displacement when it is exactly at the middle?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Zero, it is at the mean position, though the amplitude is the full 8 cm.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: 4 cm, because it has moved halfway from where it was released.

contrast_probes.probe: For a ball bouncing on the floor, is the motion SHM, and where is its displacement zero?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: It repeats, so it is SHM, with zero displacement at the middle of its bounce height.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Its displacement is zero at the floor, because that is where each bounce starts.

contrast_probes.probe: A swing's two extreme points are 2 m apart; how far is each extreme from the lowest point, and what is the amplitude?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Each extreme is 1 m from the bottom, but the amplitude is 2 m because that is the full swing.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Each extreme is 1 m from the lowest point, so the amplitude is 1 m.

contrast_probes.probe: Earth goes round the Sun once every year; is that motion SHM?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Yes, it repeats every year, so it is SHM.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: No, it is periodic, but it is not to-and-fro about a mean position with a force proportional to -x.

contrast_probes.probe: A block released 5 cm to the right of the mean position is now 2 cm to the right of it; what is its displacement?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: 3 cm, because it has moved 3 cm from where it was released.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: +2 cm, measured from the mean position.

correct_exemplars: amplitude is half the distance between the two extremes
displacement is measured from the mean position where the net force is zero
at the mean position displacement is zero and at the extremes it is plus or minus A
every SHM is periodic but not every periodic motion is SHM
it's SHM only if the restoring force is proportional to displacement and towards the mean
the release point is just an extreme, the reference is still the middle

doubts.q: Can amplitude be negative?
doubts.a: No. Amplitude is the maximum distance from the mean position, so it is always positive. Displacement can be negative, for example x = -A at the other extreme; the sign only shows which side of the mean the body is on.

doubts.q: Why do we measure displacement from the mean position and not from where we release the body?
doubts.a: The mean position is where the net force is zero, and the motion is symmetric about it, so it stays the same however you start the motion. The release point is just one extreme and can change from trial to trial.

doubts.q: Is every oscillatory motion SHM?
doubts.a: No. Oscillatory only means to-and-fro motion about a mean position. It is SHM only when the restoring force is proportional to displacement, F = -kx. A pendulum swinging through large angles oscillates but is not exactly SHM.

doubts.q: How much distance does the body cover in one complete oscillation?
doubts.a: In one oscillation it goes from the mean to one extreme, back through the mean to the other extreme, and back to the mean, covering 4A. Its displacement after one full oscillation is zero, since it returns to the same point.

name: Velocity and acceleration in SHM
subtopic: Velocity and acceleration of a particle in SHM
summary: In ideal SHM the speed is greatest at the mean position and zero at the extremes, while the acceleration is zero at the mean, greatest at the extremes, and always directed toward the mean.
learning_objective: Students will be able to state and explain where the speed and the acceleration of an ideal simple harmonic oscillator are maximum and zero, give the direction of the acceleration, and calculate v and a at any displacement.

contrast_probes.probe: Is the block's speed at the extreme position bigger than, equal to, or smaller than its speed at the mean position?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Bigger — it's fastest at the extreme.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Equal — the speed is the same everywhere.

contrast_probes.probe: What is the block's velocity at the instant it reaches the extreme position?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: It's at its highest there.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: It's zero there, so its acceleration is zero too.

contrast_probes.probe: At the mean position, is the block moving at its slowest or fastest?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Slowest — it's fastest at the ends.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Fastest, and that's why its acceleration is biggest there.

contrast_probes.probe: Does the block ever stop, even for an instant, during one oscillation?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: No, it keeps going at the same speed all the time.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Yes, at the ends it stops, so it has no acceleration there.

contrast_probes.probe: Does the block's speed change as it moves from an extreme to the mean position?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: No, it stays the same throughout.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Yes, it speeds up, and the acceleration is biggest when it reaches the mean.

contrast_probes.probe: Compare the block's acceleration at the extreme position with its acceleration at the mean position.
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: It's zero at the extreme because the block stops there.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: It's biggest at the mean because the block is fastest there.

contrast_probes.probe: Where is the block's kinetic energy largest, and where does it move fastest?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: It moves fastest at the extreme, the farthest point.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Both at the mean position, where all the energy is kinetic.

contrast_probes.probe: Does the spring's force change the block's speed during an oscillation?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: No, the speed stays constant; only the direction flips.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Yes, it speeds the block up toward the mean and slows it down beyond.

contrast_probes.probe: At the instant the block stops at an extreme, is any force acting on it?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: No, it's at rest, so there's no force and no acceleration.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Yes, the spring force is largest, so the acceleration is largest, toward the mean.

contrast_probes.probe: How much is the spring stretched when the block is at the mean position?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: It doesn't matter; the block is fastest there, so acceleration is biggest.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Not at all, so there's no force and the acceleration is zero.

correct_exemplars: Speed is greatest at the mean position because all the energy is kinetic there.
At the ends it stops for a moment, but the spring pulls hardest, so acceleration is biggest there.
Acceleration is zero in the middle because the spring isn't stretched, so there's no force.
Acceleration always points back toward the centre, proportional to how far it is from there.
It speeds up all the way to the mean and slows down after, so the speed peaks at the mean.
Zero velocity at the extreme just means it's turning around; the acceleration there is maximum.

doubts.q: How can the acceleration be maximum when the velocity is zero?
doubts.a: Acceleration measures how fast velocity changes, not how big it is. At an extreme the velocity is switching from one direction to the other, and the spring force is largest there, so the acceleration is largest even though v = 0 for an instant.

doubts.q: If the acceleration is zero at the mean position, why doesn't the block stop there?
doubts.a: Zero acceleration means the velocity is not changing at that instant, not that the velocity is zero. The block arrives at the mean with its maximum speed and carries on past it, then the restoring force starts slowing it down.

doubts.q: Is the acceleration always opposite to the velocity in SHM?
doubts.a: No. The acceleration always points toward the mean, but the velocity points toward the mean only on the way in. While moving toward the mean they are in the same direction and the body speeds up; while moving away they are opposite and it slows down.

doubts.q: Why is there a minus sign in a = −ω²x?
doubts.a: The minus sign shows the acceleration is always opposite to the displacement, that is, always directed toward the mean position. When x is positive a is negative, and when x is negative a is positive.

name: Time period, frequency and angular frequency
subtopic: Time period, frequency and angular frequency
summary: In SHM the period T = 2π/ω is fixed by the system (m and k, or L and g), not by how far it is pulled.
learning_objective: Students will be able to convert between T, f and ω, calculate the period of a spring–mass system and a simple pendulum, and explain why the period does not depend on amplitude in ideal SHM.

contrast_probes.probe: Two pendulums of equal length: a light bob pulled far and a heavy bob pulled a little. Which one do you think takes longer per swing, and what decides it?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: The light bob, because it is pulled further and has more distance to cover.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: It depends on the bobs' masses; the heavy one will be slower or faster because of its weight.

contrast_probes.probe: A block with ω = 2π rad/s is pulled from 5 cm to 10 cm. What is its period now, and why?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: It was 1 s, but now it travels double the distance, so about 2 s.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Period is 1 by omega, so 1/(2π), about 0.16 s, whatever the amplitude.

contrast_probes.probe: A spring–mass system has ω = 4π rad/s. What extra information, if any, do you need to find its period?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: I need the mass of the block, otherwise I can't find the period.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Nothing extra; the period is 1/ω = 1/(4π) s.

contrast_probes.probe: If you double the amplitude of a spring–mass oscillator, what happens to the time for one oscillation?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: It increases, because the block has to cover more distance.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: It stays the same; the block covers more distance but moves faster, and T = 2π√(m/k) has no amplitude.

contrast_probes.probe: You replace a 100 g bob with a 400 g bob on a pendulum, and a 100 g block with a 400 g block on a spring. What happens to each period?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Either both periods change because of the extra mass, or neither changes because only L and k matter.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: The pendulum's period stays the same, but the spring's period doubles because T ∝ √m.

contrast_probes.probe: An oscillator has ω = 10π rad/s. How many full oscillations does it make in one second?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: 10π, about 31 oscillations, since omega is the frequency.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: 5, because f = ω/2π = 10π/2π.

correct_exemplars: period is 2 pi by omega because one cycle is 2 pi radians
amplitude isn't in the formula so the period stays the same
pendulum period depends only on length and g, the mass cancels
for a spring T is 2 pi root m by k so four times mass gives double period
bigger swing means more distance but also more speed, so same time
f is omega by 2 pi, so 4 pi radians per second is 2 hertz

doubts.q: Why do we need both f and ω if they both tell how fast it oscillates?
doubts.a: f counts full oscillations per second, while ω counts radians of phase per second. ω fits naturally into x = A cos(ωt + φ) and into ω = √(k/m). They are linked by ω = 2πf.

doubts.q: Why does a pendulum's period not depend on the mass of the bob, but a spring's period does?
doubts.a: In a pendulum the restoring force comes from gravity, which grows with mass, so mass cancels with inertia. In a spring the restoring force kx does not depend on the block's mass, so a heavier block accelerates less and T = 2π√(m/k) grows.

doubts.q: Is the pendulum period really independent of amplitude for any swing?
doubts.a: Only for small angles, where sin θ ≈ θ and the motion is SHM. For large swings the period becomes slightly longer than 2π√(L/g).

doubts.q: If I double the mass on a spring, why does the period not double?
doubts.a: The period depends on the square root of mass, T = 2π√(m/k). Doubling m multiplies T by √2 ≈ 1.41; you need four times the mass to double the period.

name: Restoring force and a = −ω²x
subtopic: Restoring force and the defining condition a = −ω²x
summary: In SHM the restoring force F = −kx grows with displacement and always points toward the mean position, so a = −ω²x with ω² = k/m.
learning_objective: Students will be able to state that the restoring force in SHM is proportional to displacement and always directed toward the mean position, and use a = −ω²x with ω² = k/m to find acceleration at any displacement.

contrast_probes.probe: As the block moves from the mean out to the extreme, what happens to the restoring force?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Nothing changes, it's the same force all the way out.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: It keeps pushing the block outward, that's why it reaches the extreme.

contrast_probes.probe: How does the restoring force at 1 cm from the mean compare with the force at 4 cm?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: They're equal, the spring is the same so the force is the same.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: At 4 cm it's four times bigger, since F is proportional to x.

contrast_probes.probe: While the block is moving outward, past the mean toward the extreme, which way does the force on it point?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Outward, along with the motion.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Back toward the mean, which is why the block slows down and stops at the extreme.

correct_exemplars: force always points back toward the mean position
F equals minus kx, so it's opposite to displacement and grows with it
double the displacement, double the restoring force
acceleration is minus omega squared x, always toward the centre
at the mean the force is zero, at the extremes it's maximum
even while it's moving outward, the force is pulling it back to the mean

doubts.q: If the force always pulls toward the mean, why doesn't the block just stop at the mean?
doubts.a: At the mean the force is zero but the speed is maximum. By inertia the block overshoots, and only then does the restoring force start slowing it down on the other side.

doubts.q: What does the minus sign in F = −kx actually mean?
doubts.a: It means the force is opposite to the displacement. If x is positive the force is negative, and vice versa, so the force always points back to the mean.

doubts.q: At the extreme the velocity is zero, so isn't the acceleration also zero there?
doubts.a: No. Acceleration depends on displacement, not velocity. At the extreme x = ±A, so the acceleration has its largest magnitude, ω²A, directed toward the mean.

doubts.q: Is every to-and-fro motion SHM?
doubts.a: No. It is SHM only if the acceleration is proportional to displacement and opposite to it, a = −ω²x. A ball bouncing on the floor is periodic but not SHM, because its acceleration is g, which does not depend on x.

name: Energy in SHM
summary: In ideal SHM, kinetic and potential energy keep trading places, but their sum stays fixed at ½kA².
learning_objective: Students will be able to find the kinetic, potential and total energy of a body in SHM at any displacement, and explain why the total stays constant and grows as the square of the amplitude.

contrast_probes.probe: At the mean position, how much energy is stored in the spring, and is the block's total energy there more than, less than, or equal to its total at the extreme?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: The spring's PE is zero at the mean, but the total is more there because the block is moving fastest.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: The spring's PE is maximum at the mean, along with the KE, so that's where the energy is biggest.

contrast_probes.probe: For a block on a spring, does the total energy depend on its position during the motion, on the amplitude, or on both?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: It depends on position: more energy near the middle and less near the ends.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: It depends on the amplitude, in direct proportion: twice the amplitude, twice the energy.

contrast_probes.probe: If the amplitude doubles, what happens to the PE at the mean position and to the total energy?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: The PE at the mean, which is its biggest value, goes up, since a bigger swing stores more there.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: The total energy doubles because energy follows the amplitude directly.

contrast_probes.probe: As the block slows down near the extreme, where does its kinetic energy go?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: It is lost, so the block has less total energy near the extreme.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: It goes into the stretched spring as PE, so the total stays the same.

contrast_probes.probe: At which position is the spring stretched or compressed the most, and what does that mean for the PE there?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: The mean is the key point, so PE should be maximum there, along with the KE.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: The stretch is greatest at the extremes, so PE = ½kx² is maximum there and zero at the mean.

contrast_probes.probe: If the amplitude is made three times larger, by what factor does the total energy change?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Three times, since energy goes with the amplitude.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Nine times, since E = ½kA² and 3² = 9.

correct_exemplars: the total stays the same, KE just turns into PE and back
PE is maximum at the extremes and KE is maximum at the mean
E is half k A square, so doubling A makes it four times
at any point KE plus PE equals half k A square
at the mean the spring is not stretched so PE is zero and KE is full
with no friction nothing is lost, so the total energy is constant

doubts.q: If the total energy is constant, why does a real spring or pendulum eventually stop?
doubts.a: Real systems have friction and air drag, which slowly turn mechanical energy into heat. That is damped oscillation, and the amplitude shrinks. E = ½kA² stays constant only in the ideal, undamped case.

doubts.q: At what displacement are KE and PE equal?
doubts.a: Set ½kx² = ½ × ½kA², so x² = A²/2 and x = ±A/√2 ≈ ±0.707A. There each energy is half the total.

doubts.q: Does the total energy depend on the mass if I use E = ½mω²A²?
doubts.a: For a given spring, k = mω² is fixed, so E = ½kA² depends only on k and A. Changing the mass changes ω but not the energy for the same amplitude. Mass appears in ½mω²A² only because ω itself depends on m.

doubts.q: How often do KE and PE repeat compared to the motion itself?
doubts.a: KE is maximum each time the body passes the mean, which happens twice per cycle. So KE and PE each repeat with period T/2, or frequency 2f, while the total stays flat.

name: Refraction and total internal reflection
subtopic: Refraction at a plane surface and total internal reflection
summary: Light bends toward the normal entering a denser medium, away entering a rarer one; TIR needs denser-to-rarer travel beyond the critical angle.
learning_objective: Predict whether a ray bends toward or away from the normal, use n = c/v and Snell's law, and decide when total internal reflection can occur.

contrast_probes.probe: A ray from air hits a pond at 70° to the normal, more than water's critical angle. What happens to it at the surface?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: You expect it to enter and bend toward the normal; good, but would you say the same for a ray leaving water into air?
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: You expect it to be totally reflected; check which side of the surface the light starts on, and where it is denser.

contrast_probes.probe: A ray inside glass meets the glass-air surface at 20°. In the air, is its angle from the normal bigger or smaller than 20°?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: You said smaller; ask yourself whether air is denser or rarer than glass, and what that does to the bending.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: You said bigger; now, what would happen if that 20° grew past about 42°?

contrast_probes.probe: Can light coming from the air ever be totally internally reflected at a glass surface if you make the angle big enough?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: You said yes; try it in the refraction visual from the air side at 80° and see whether any beam goes into the glass.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: You said no; so what two things must be true for light to get trapped inside the glass?

contrast_probes.probe: Draw the normal where the ray meets the surface. Which angle goes into Snell's law: the one with the surface or the one with that line?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: The angle with the surface.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: The angle with the normal.

contrast_probes.probe: Before deciding which way the ray bends, which line do you measure its angle from?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: From the surface.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: From the normal, and it always ends up closer to the normal.

contrast_probes.probe: A ray makes 60° with a glass surface from the air side. Can it be totally internally reflected, and which angle do you use to check?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: I use 60° in Snell's law.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Yes, if the angle is big enough it reflects whatever the direction.

correct_exemplars: denser to rarer it bends away, rarer to denser it bends toward
TIR only works going from the denser side out to the rarer side
you need denser to rarer and the angle bigger than critical, both
coming out of water into air it goes away from the normal
air into glass can never be TIR, it always gets in
if it hits straight along the normal it doesn't bend at all

doubts.q: Does the colour (frequency) of light change when it enters water?
doubts.a: No. Frequency is set by the source and stays the same in every medium. Speed and wavelength both drop by the factor n, which is why a red laser still looks red underwater.

doubts.q: Why doesn't light bend when it hits the surface along the normal?
doubts.a: At 0° incidence, sin i = 0, so Snell's law gives sin r = 0 and the ray goes straight on. It still slows down; only its direction is unchanged.

doubts.q: Can total internal reflection happen when light goes from air into glass?
doubts.a: No. Going from rarer to denser, sin r = sin i / n is always less than 1, so a refracted ray always exists. TIR needs light in the denser medium heading toward a rarer one beyond the critical angle.

doubts.q: Why is it called 'total' if some light reflects at every surface anyway?
doubts.a: Below the critical angle a surface reflects a small part and refracts the rest. Beyond it there is no refracted ray at all, so all the light is reflected, which is why optical fibres lose so little light.

name: Lenses and image formation
subtopic: Thin lenses: lens formula and image formation
summary: A convex lens forms a full real image where rays meet, screen or not.
learning_objective: Use 1/v − 1/u = 1/f and m = v/u to locate the image formed by a convex lens, and explain why covering part of the lens or removing the screen does not remove a real image.

contrast_probes.probe: Half the lens is covered and the screen is taken away. What is left at the spot where the image was?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Half an image is still there at that spot.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Nothing at all, because the screen is gone.

contrast_probes.probe: The image is sharp on the screen. You stick paper over the top half of the lens. What changes on the screen?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Part of the image disappears and only half is left.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: The whole image stays but gets dimmer.

contrast_probes.probe: You remove the screen and put your eye some distance beyond where the image was, looking at the lens. Do you see the image?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: No, without the screen there is nothing to see.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Yes, I see the inverted image hanging in the air.

correct_exemplars: the full image still forms, just dimmer, because every part of the lens gets light from every point
the rays still meet at the same spot even if there's no screen
covering half the lens cuts the light, not the picture
the screen just lets us see it, the image is there anyway
half the lens means less light, so a fainter but complete image
if you put your eye beyond the image you could see it in the air

doubts.q: If I cover half the lens, why doesn't half the image vanish?
doubts.a: Each point of the object sends rays to the whole lens. The open half still collects rays from every point and brings them to the same image points, so the image is complete but dimmer.

doubts.q: How can a real image exist if there is no screen?
doubts.a: A real image is where rays actually meet. They meet there and spread out again; a screen only scatters that light toward your eyes. An eye placed beyond the image, inside the cone of rays, sees it in mid-air.

doubts.q: Why is u negative in the lens formula?
doubts.a: In the Cartesian sign convention, distances are measured from the optical centre and are positive along the incident light. A real object sits on the side the light comes from, so u is negative. Confirm the convention your textbook uses.

doubts.q: What does a negative v or a negative m mean?
doubts.a: Negative v means the image is on the same side as the object: virtual, upright and not catchable on a screen. Negative m means the image is inverted; for a single convex lens this goes with positive v.
